name: John Rufus
knownFor: Disciple of Peter the Iberian and bishop of Maiuma near Gaza, whose Plerophories gather stories and visions told against the council of Chalcedon.
dates: Ordained priest at Antioch between 476 and 478 and wrote soon after 512, both by François Nau's account. In Jerusalem in 485, Nau says
place: Southern Palestine, probably Ascalon, by Nau's account; Beirut, Antioch, Jerusalem, and Maiuma near Gaza
tradition: The Church of Alexandria and Miaphysite Egypt
role: Priest, then bishop of Maiuma; collector of the Plerophories

keyWorks.title: Plerophories (Testimonies and Revelations against the Council of Chalcedon)
keyWorks.about: 89 short chapters of visions, wonders and prophecies, most of them told by Peter the Iberian, written in Greek soon after 512 by Nau's account and surviving in Syriac

traces: Nau: the Plerophories were used by the writer of the History of Dioscorus by his disciple Theopistus, and Michael the Syrian summed up nearly all their chapters in his chronicle.
Nau: the book shows how the anti-Chalcedonians, then in power between 512 and 518, saw the council of Chalcedon.
remembered: The heading of the Syriac text, in Nau's French, names the author as one of Peter the Iberian's disciples, the priest "Jean de Beit-Rufin, d'Antioche", bishop of "Maiouma de Gaza".
Zachariah of Mitylene, in his Life of Severus, says he had studied law at Beirut with Theodore and left a name there for chastity and piety.

uncertain: His life rests on François Nau's reading of the few chapters where he speaks of himself, and on Zachariah of Mitylene's Life of Severus. Nau works out the dates of his ordination and of the book from the book itself.
Nau says he succeeded Peter the Iberian as bishop of Maiuma. Zachariah says only that the altar was kept for him after Peter died, while Theodore and John the Canopite led the monastery.

The Life of Peter the Iberian names no author. Richard Raabe, its German editor, says the name was already unknown in the time of Evagrius of Epiphania, and leaves open whether the author of the Plerophories is the same man.

The Plerophories are partisan. Nau calls them a new kind of collection of sayings, written to fight the council of Chalcedon and its defenders, and says their sources are oral, with a written witness very rarely cited.
The card's tradition is the era 3 scan's placing; he worked in Palestine, under Peter the Fuller of Antioch and Peter the Iberian.
